title: Two-port amplifier models and loading in cascades

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A **two-port model** compresses an amplifier into three numbers: an input resistance, a controlled source, and an output resistance. Once you have them, you can predict the gain with any source and any load without reanalysing the transistors. The controlled source can be written as a voltage gain (Thevenin output) or a transconductance (Norton output); the two are related by \(A_v = -G_mR_{out}\).

Each port resistance is found with a test source. Zero the independent input source but keep its resistance, keep every dependent source, apply \(v_t\) and measure \(i_t\). The payoff is **loading**. The source resistance and \(R_{in}\) form a divider at the input, and \(R_{out}\) and the load form one at the output. Between cascaded stages the same divider appears at every interface. For voltage gain you want \(R_{in}\) high and \(R_{out}\) low; a current amplifier wants the opposite. That is why buffers and current stages exist.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ \frac{v_{out}}{v_s} = \frac{R_{in}}{R_s + R_{in}}\cdot A_v\cdot\frac{R_L}{R_{out} + R_L}, \qquad A_v = -G_mR_{out} \]
\[ R_{in} = \frac{v_t}{i_t}\Big|_{\text{input}}, \qquad R_{out} = \frac{v_t}{i_t}\Big|_{\text{output},\ v_s = 0} \]

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: An amplifier with \(R_{in} = 25\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(A_v = 30\) and \(R_{out} = 3\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) is driven from a 5 kΩ source into a 6 kΩ load. The input divider is \(25/30 = 0.833\) and the output divider is \(6/9 = 0.667\), so the gain is \(0.833\times30\times0.667 = 16.7\), barely half the unloaded value.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Quoting the open-circuit gain as if no source or load were attached.
- Zeroing the dependent source when finding \(R_{out}\).
- Matching resistances "for maximum transfer" when voltage gain is the goal.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Every single-stage amplifier (CS, CG, CD) gets reduced to a two-port. Cascades are then multiplied out one divider at a time.
